Dropping "help" upgrades a contributory-role statement into a flat prevention claim — Wallach said these amino acids help prevent cancer, the summary says they prevent it. Everything else in the claim is faithful: the amino-acid list, the respective disease pairing (arginine→cancer, taurine→macular degeneration, tyrosine→goiter), "over the long haul," and the "classic essential amino acids" framing all match the verbatim and the surrounding span. No injected outside facts, no number/unit conflict, no inversion, no misattribution.

fixes.verifier_why:
The reviewer is right, and the fix is minimum-force. Verbatim confirmed byte-faithful against source_span_pm3500 (exact match incl. line breaks): "Over the long haul, these three amino acids HELP PREVENT certain specific diseases. Respectively, those diseases are cancer, macular degeneration, and goiter." The original claim_text renders this as "over the long haul preventing cancer, macular degeneration, and goiter respectively" — dropping "help".

Why this is a real defect and not an over-eager rewrite: "help prevent" vs "prevent" is not stylistic compression, it is the difference between a contributory-role statement and a flat causal disease-prevention claim. In this exact domain that hedge is load-bearing — it is the standard structure-function qualifier, and §00.A's legal-defensibility purpose ("every claim attributable, not invented") is precisely about not shipping a stronger claim than Wallach made under Wallach's name. "Over the long haul" carries a temporal hedge, not a contributory one, so it does not absorb the lost meaning.

Adversarial check for over-eagerness — the proposed edit restores ONE word and touches nothing else. Everything the reviewer certified as faithful I independently confirmed against the span: the three-amino-acid list, the respective pairing (arginine→cancer, taurine→macular degeneration, tyrosine→goiter, matching the claim's conditions[] order), "classic essential amino acids", and "over the long haul". No outside facts injected, no dose/unit involved (dose: null), no inversion, no misattribution — Wallach speaks in first person ("I would add"), correctly attributed. The rewrite adds nothing not in the verbatim and removes nothing that was faithful, so it is not the strengthen-by-paraphrase failure mode this review guards against.

No escalation needed: page_image_available is false, but no image is required — the span fully contains and confirms the verbatim, so the discrepancy is resolvable from text alone. Note for the record (out of scope, no action proposed): essentials[] is ordered ["arginine","tyrosine","taurine"] while the respective mapping runs arginine/taurine/tyrosine — harmless since essentials[] is an unordered set and the respective pairing lives in claim_text, but worth an eye if any consumer ever zips essentials[] against conditions[] positionally.

fixes.verifier_why: Verified independently; the reviewer is correct and the fix is minimal, not over-eager. (1) Word-boundary search of source_span_pm3500 returns ZERO hits for \bsteroid\b. An initial 9-hit count for "sterol" was a false signal — it is a substring of "chole-sterol"; the real standalone hits are "sterols" (x2) and "steer" (x1). (2) Wallach's own taxonomy sentence reads "Cholesterol is a member of a large group of fats known as sterols" — he applies "sterols" to the FAT GROUP cholesterol belongs to, never to the hormones. So the original did not merely omit his word, it substituted a different technical category he never used: outside knowledge injected as Wallach, the corpus's flagged cardinal defect. The two defects compound: adrenal cortical hormones are themselves steroids, so the injected definite-article label ("the steroid hormones") creates a bucket the dropped item belongs to, making the truncation invisible — a reader concludes Wallach named three hormones under a category, when he named four hormone-class items under no category. I weighed the strongest counterargument, that the summary layer permits modern voice, and reject it: that standard is scoped to UNITS (mg% to mg/dL, cc to mL), a lossless re-expression of a value Wallach gave, whereas adding a taxonomic classification asserts a world-fact under his name — and here the word is not even span-present. I also checked the proposed edit for the opposite failure and it smuggles in nothing: every clause maps to source, the six-item list is preserved in source order, and it strictly moves claim_text toward the verbatim by removing an injected word and restoring dropped items. Not escalated: the verbatim is byte-present inside the span (confirmed True), so the source text is not in question and no page image is needed. Blast radius is low — dose is null, essentials and conditions untouched, no number, unit, or attribution affected. Reviewer was honest that this is MINOR and non-dangerous, but minor governs urgency, not whether it is a defect.

fixes.verifier_why: The original genuinely misrepresents the source; this is not an over-eager rewrite. fixes.concern: The closing clause injects an argument absent from the source span: "He offers this as evidence that real animal fats like butter belong in a healthy traditional diet — the opposite of the processed substitutes modern medicine pushed in their place." The span is a neutral descriptive enumeration ("There are 14 Hunza practices that contribute to their longevity") with no mention of processed substitutes, margarine, or modern medicine, and no polemical framing. Attributing that contrast to Wallach *here* imports a stance he makes elsewhere in the corpus but not in this passage. Minor secondary: "daily staple" firms the span's "Dairy, including whole milk, buttermilk, yogurt, cheese, and butter, are staples" into a daily frequency the span states only for wine and salt.
fixes.proposed_edit: Yes — emphatically. In Wallach's account of the Hunza, the people he describes as relatively disease-free and living well past a hundred, butter is a staple rather than an afterthought: they put it in their tea and use it as a cooking shortening, and it sits among their core fat sources alongside whole milk, ghee, apricot oil and animal fats. He lists those fat sources as one of the 14 Hunza practices that contribute to their longevity. In his words: "Fat sources include whole milk, butter, ghee, apricot oil, and animal fats."
fixes.verifier_why: The original genuinely misrepresents the span. Its closing clause — "He offers this as evidence that real animal fats like butter belong in a healthy traditional diet — the opposite of the processed substitutes modern medicine pushed in their place" — has zero anchor in the source: token scan of the full span returns margarine 0, substitut* 0, "modern medicine" 0, "vegetable oil" 0, hydrogenat* 0. The two nearest passages are topically disjoint — item 13's "no processed or white flours" concerns flour, and item 10's "western style hospitals or doctors / high tech health practitioners" concerns medical care, not dietary fat. Fusing them into a claim that modern medicine pushed processed fat substitutes in place of animal fats is a cross-topic synthesis Wallach does not perform in this passage, which is a neutral descriptive enumeration ("There are 14 Hunza practices that contribute to their longevity"). Because that polemic IS a genuine Wallach stance elsewhere in DDDL, this is the outside-knowledge-injected-as-wallach failure class rather than a stylistic quibble: a reader following the claim to its verbatim finds only a five-item list of fat sources, so the claim attributes an argument to a location where none exists — directly against §00.A's attributable-not-invented purpose. Secondary point also holds, minor: "daily" occurs twice in the span and both are deliberate ("A grape wine known as Pani is consumed daily"; item 6 "Daily consumption of salt"), while butter gets only "staples" with no frequency, so "daily staple" borrows a word the source withholds here. The replacement injects nothing new — every element traces (disease-free/past-a-hundred → item 11; tea + cooking shortening → the dairy sentence, and it corrects the original's tense drift "used" → the span's "use"; fat sources → the verbatim; "one of the 14 Hunza practices that contribute to their longevity" → the span header plus item 4's position). Verbatim confirmed byte-present in span. "Yes — emphatically" survives and is defensible on butter's threefold repetition within the span. This is a subtraction of injected argument plus a firming-down, not an over-eager rewrite of a faithful claim.

fixes.concern: Two source-grounded defects plus one overstated derived comparison. (1) INJECTED outside-world fact: claim_text states "tuna in particular is a large predator fish that concentrates mercury — making it a poor way to chase germanium." Nothing in the ±3500-char span mentions mercury, predator fish, or any caution about eating fish; the span's only fish content is the bare datum "tuna—2.3 ppm". The mercury/bioaccumulation point is true in the world but is not Wallach's word here, and it is presented as part of the source-grounded answer. (2) QUALIFIER-SHIFT: the source reads "A severely reduced immune status ... typify deficiencies of germanium"; claim_text softens this to "weakened immunity", dropping "severely". (3) Overstated multiple: "hundreds of times less than the germanium-rich foods ... (100 to 2,000 ppm)" — against tuna's 2.3 ppm the actual ratio spans 43x to 870x, so "hundreds of times" is wrong at the low end of the range the claim itself cites. Everything else checks out exactly: the NK-cell/interferon/macrophage immune mechanism, the oxygen-utilization cofactor role, beans 4.67 ppm, tuna 2.3 ppm, and the 100-2,000 ppm herb range all match the span verbatim.
fixes.proposed_edit: Yes, but only a trace — and it is not a reason to eat tuna. Germanium is a trace element Wallach prizes as an immune booster (it stimulates natural killer cells, interferon, macrophages and T-suppressor cells) and an oxygen-utilization cofactor, with deficiency typified by a severely reduced immune status, arthritis, osteoporosis, low energy and cancer. But tuna carries only about 2.3 ppm of germanium — actually less than ordinary beans at 4.67 ppm, and far below the germanium-rich healing herbs and foods like garlic, ginseng and shiitake mushrooms (100 to 2,000 ppm). So fish is a minor incidental source at best — not a meaningful way to get germanium. In his words: "tuna—2.3 ppm"
fixes.verifier_why:
All three charges CONFIRMED against the full 7,000-char span; charge 1 alone is decisive and is not a stylistic quibble.

(1) INJECTED OUTSIDE FACT — the controlling defect. Mechanical grep over the whole span returns ZERO hits for mercury/Mercury/Hg/predator/bioaccum; the token "fish" does not appear anywhere, and the only fish content is the bare datum "tuna-2.3 ppm". (The four "concentrat" hits are gadolinium in land plants and hydrogen-ion concentration pH regulation - unrelated.) The original's closing clause "tuna in particular is a large predator fish that concentrates mercury - making it a poor way to chase germanium" is a causal mechanism PLUS a recommendation, presented inside the source-grounded answer under Wallach's attribution, with no basis in the span. This is the project's flagged cardinal defect class (outside-knowledge-injected-as-wallach: true-in-world facts that are not in the book). It resolves without a page image: even if Wallach discusses mercury elsewhere in DDDL, it cannot ride on THIS claim's verbatim, which is solely "Food plants and animals contain small amounts of germanium (i.e. beans-4.67 ppm, tuna-2.3 ppm)" - a mercury caution would require its own claim with its own verbatim. Hence keep-change, not escalate.

(2) QUALIFIER-SHIFT confirmed. Source: "A severely reduced immune status, arthritis, osteoporosis, low energy, and cancer typify deficiencies of germanium." Original softened to "weakened immunity", dropping "severely". The edit restores the source's own qualifier. Minor but real, and the fix is strictly toward the source.

(3) OVERSTATED MULTIPLE confirmed by arithmetic: 100/2.3 = 43.5x, 2000/2.3 = 869.6x. "Hundreds of times less" is falsified by the very range the claim itself cites (100 to 2,000 ppm) - it is tens at the low end. The replacement "far below" is accurate across the whole range.

ADVERSARIAL CHECK FOR OVER-EAGER REWRITE - the edit does NOT over-reach. Every change moves toward the source and none adds unsourced content: "T-suppressor cells" is source-present ("...natural killer cells, lymphokines such as IFN(y) interferon, macrophages, and T-suppresser cells") and was MISSING from the original, so the edit increases source fidelity rather than embellishing; "healing herbs and foods" matches "Healing herbs such as"; the oxygen-utilization cofactor role ("acts as a metallic cofactor for oxygen utilization"), beans 4.67 ppm, tuna 2.3 ppm, and the 100-2,000 ppm herb range all match the span exactly. The verbatim field is untouched and was verified byte-contained in the span (normalized match = True). The retained opener "not a reason to eat tuna" is, in the edited version, grounded purely in the in-span ppm comparison (tuna below ordinary beans, far below the herbs) rather than the removed mercury caution, so it reads as "tuna is not a meaningful germanium source" - an in-span derivation - not as a health warning. The mild tuna-to-"fish" generalization is supported by the verbatim's own "Food plants and animals contain small amounts of germanium".

The original genuinely misrepresents the source on the item that matters most, so the default-to-revert presumption is overcome.

WHAT IT IS: fluoride is the most reactive halogen and, per a 1972 study by Schwarz, a nutritionally essential trace mineral for animals and humans. ITS REAL BENEFIT: fluoride hardens tooth enamel — teeth rebuild it as acid-resistant fluorapatite, which fights the cavities caused by sugar-fed mouth bacteria; that is why it's in toothpaste, and water fluoridation (~1 mg/L) has reportedly cut cavities 60–70%. ITS REAL HARMS: fluoride is also toxic above trace levels — dental fluorosis (mottled teeth) at 2–7 ppm, osteosclerosis (abnormal bone hardening) at 8–20 ppm, and chronic systemic toxicity above 20–80 ppm/day over years — and Wallach cites studies (Yiamouyiannis & Burk 1977; the U.S. National Toxicology Program's 1990 rat study) tying fluoridation to excess cancer deaths and to oral, bone (osteosarcoma), thyroid and liver tumors. Fluoride is essential only in tiny amounts (skeletal reserves in an adult man can reach 2.6 g; the average daily intake by Americans is 4.4 mg), while the harms appear at higher, sustained exposure — so 'essential in trace' and 'toxic in excess' are the same mineral at different doses, not a contradiction. Helium is second only to hydrogen as the most abundant element in the universe: it makes up seven percent of all the existing atoms, and together helium and hydrogen make up 99.9% of elements in the universe. Almost all of the helium gas on Earth is found in "natural gas," produced by the decay of uranium and radon radioactive isotopes (the common name for these helium nuclei is "alpha particles," named by their discoverer Sir Ernest Rutherford).
